speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: asked the Minister for National Development (a) what are the considerations as to whether or not a green space can be protected as a nature reserve; and (b) whether this has been considered for the Dover Forest.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: asked the Minister for National Development (a) what are the new trends factored in the current review of the Concept Plan; (b) whether there is a minimum percentage requirement of Singapore's land space to be allocated for natural green space such as forests; and (c) whether COVID-19 has affected the considerations of future land use in terms of natural and built environment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I will first address our overall approach to land use planning and nature conservation, and then talk about specific sites and locations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are a city, 728 sq km of land area in all.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our land use considerations are therefore quite different from most other cities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is because, unlike most other cities which have large hinterlands, we have to cater for everything that a country needs within the limits of our city, instead of far beyond its limits in the case of other cities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These include things such as airports and seaports, airbases and military training ground, reservoirs, incineration and power plants, agriculture and so much more.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our approach to conservation as a city-state is also quite different.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, in other cities, you travel out, sometimes for many hours on the motorway, to enjoy natural greenery and nature.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But in Singapore, our wild spaces are right in our midst, with our gem, the Central Catchment and Bukit Timah Nature Reserves, nestled in the green heart of our city.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have always taken a long-term view towards land use planning, with stewardship and sustainability as core, long-held principles.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Given our small size, we have been, and have to be, judicious in stewarding our scarce land resources to support Singapore’s development as well as in our aspiration to be a City in Nature.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have to constantly balance demands and trade-offs across a wide variety of needs, including housing, green spaces, infrastructure, community facilities, workplaces, amongst others.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These tensions are inherent in land use planning everywhere, but felt more acutely in a small city-state like Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Sustainable development for Singapore over the long term also means that we need to recycle and reuse our limited land, while incorporating flexibility into our plans, to meet the changing needs and aspirations of each new generation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We must continue to plan ahead to support our collective vision for Singapore, not just for ourselves, but for our children and theirs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our land use needs today are quite different from those of yesteryear, and will continue to evolve.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Today, we continue to see a high demand for new HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This means that for each BTO flat, we broadly get between five and six Singaporean applicants.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is driven partly by marriage and family formation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In the near term, we expect more demand from the larger "Echo" Baby Boomers cohorts – born in the late 1980s to 1990s – as they enter into marriageable age.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For completeness, other housing options, including HDB resale flats, ECs, private property, open market rental flats or living with family members, remain.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, therefore, we need to continue building to meet the demands and aspirations of young families.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And I am sure Members, from time to time, at your Meet-the-People Sessions or, more likely, via email, Facebook, Instagram and LinkedIn, they will reach out to you.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: On top of that, our public housing demand is also partly driven by changing social structures.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, there is a growing trend of smaller households as more young couples, singles and their parents choose to have their own flats and their own homes instead of staying with their extended families, as it was so in the past.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Indeed, Members of this House have championed some of these needs and more.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Or take a more recent development like COVID-19, which continues to impact our lives in many significant ways, and has thrown up new land use challenges.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Apart from the fact that working from home became the norm for many of us, the pandemic also reminded us that supply disruptions are a very real concern.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, given the supply tightness that the world experienced for certain food and medical items, our agencies are looking to strengthen local resilience of some of our resource systems, such as for food.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This may mean increasing local production and storage capacity for such resources, where feasible.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The pandemic has also demonstrated the importance of having buffer sites for emergency uses, which we were able to activate quickly for quarantine and recovery facilities, and temporary housing of our migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Meanwhile, trends such as tele-commuting and e-commerce have accelerated, raising questions about how much office and retail space we might really need in the long term.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our economic imperatives may also shift and evolve after the pandemic as technology changes and advances, so we will need to take a good, hard look at land use needs for the future.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: While it remains to be seen if some of these shifts will persist in the "new normal" beyond COVID-19, we are actively monitoring these trends and adjusting our land use strategies to satisfy both the needs of today and the possibilities and challenges of tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To meet our growing and changing needs, we have been, and will continue to adopt a range of development options.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This includes increasing the density of developments – building higher and building more densely, while ensuring liveability.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, the upcoming Punggol Town Hub will feature a public library, community centre, hawker centre and health services, all co-located, some stacked on top of each other, for one-stop, convenient access for our residents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This, of course, beats having one site for the CC, one site for the hawker centre, one site for the healthcare services, one site for the library, and so on and so forth.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are also co-locating a Water Reclamation Plant and an Integrated Waste Management Facility at Tuas Nexus, and a four-in-one rail and bus depot in the East Coast.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Such projects save us hectares of land that can be used for other purposes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are also redeveloping brownfield sites such as golf courses, old school sites, or industrial areas, as leases expire.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, last year, we launched the former First Toa Payoh Secondary School site for public housing, after the school was merged.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Many Members might also remember that Bishan used to be a cemetery.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Going forward, when the lease for the Keppel Club Golf Course expires, we will use the land to develop public and private housing.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Land taken back from Jurong Country Club, Raffles Country Club, Marina Bay Golf Course from 2024 and Orchid Country Club from 2030, will also be used to meet other needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We will continue to carry out land reclamation where appropriate and see how we can also make use of underground spaces and deep cavern spaces for infrastructure, though the costs are high.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If you look at the geological map of Singapore, parts of it are granite, solid hard rock; parts of it are sedimentary rock.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In fact, a number of years ago, I visited the Jurong Rock Caverns at Jurong Island, which makes use of cavernous underground space, through advances in engineering, to store high-value products, saving the surface for other uses.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We also undertake major long-term strategic redevelopment moves whenever the opportunity arises – an opportunity to re-imagine Singapore, to advance our children's interests and that of their grandchildren.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But many of these moves take time and require complex planning and careful coordination, because they affect people, homes, livelihoods and industries.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, we cannot redevelop these spaces overnight but plan far, far ahead, like now, for the needs of the next generation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There are also different trade-offs to weigh, including the compatibility of a new development with surrounding land uses, and the availability and capacity of supporting infrastructure, among other considerations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Now, let me move on and explain our approach when it comes to greenfield sites, vegetated sites, green and natural areas.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Because of our commitment to land stewardship and sustainable development, we adopt a science-based approach to identify core biodiversity areas and surrounding buffers that we want to retain for future generations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Broadly, the considerations include ecological significance and ecological connectivity of habitats.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The four-pronged Nature Conservation Masterplan sets out the strategies to safeguard these green spaces.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In fact, the Masterplan goes much more than that; in terms of City in Nature, it is also the mindset of people, their ability to be conscious about nature, to be scientific about it, and also to be able to understand all the stresses and tensions we deal with, as we seek to protect biodiversity on our city island.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As a result of this approach, we have retained a number of ecologically important sites as green spaces, although they had initially been designated for other uses, human uses.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For instance, the Mandai Mangrove and Mudflat had initially been planned for factory use, for industry.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Yet, after careful study through biodiversity surveys and ecological modelling, we decided to keep it as a Nature Park given its high ecological value, both domestically as well as playing our role internationally as part of a flyway.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Similarly, while other green spaces such as Dairy Farm Nature Park and Rifle Range Nature Park could have been developed for housing, they have been retained as green buffers to our Nature Reserves instead.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And we have done this in many other areas too over time – Sungei Buloh, Pulau Ubin and Chek Jawa, Kranji Marshes, Chestnut, Thomson, Khatib Bongsu, Bukit Batok Hillside Nature Park, Admiralty Park, Hampstead Wetland Park, Tampines Eco Green, Tampines Quarry, Rail Corridor, to name a few.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are looking out for more areas to help enhance ecological connectivity; and we have to look at those areas with biodiversity and significant biological importance, and prioritise those.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These comprise key representative eco-systems and habitats for Singapore’s native biodiversity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We need to also remember that not all of these areas were untouched habitats.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, Sungei Buloh Wetland Reserve and the upcoming Khatib Bongsu Nature Park were once prawn farming areas.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These areas were abandoned, the land was acquired by Government in days gone by for future redevelopment, and they were marked out by earlier batches of leaders and public officers for our generation's use, and the next generation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I seek all Members' support when we intensify in your areas.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: These efforts will restore existing ecological habitats for our wildlife and provide Singaporeans with greater access and a more immersive experience in nature.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And so, it is not just the green space that we protect but we intensify it, for example, through the Forest Restoration Action Plan.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: When you go into a green space, you look at the mix of native and alien invasive species, you look at what might be strangling the forest and ecology, what may be disrupting the habitat, even though it looks all green from afar.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, in the Bukit Timah area, the Rifle Range area, painstaking removal of Dioscorea by hand and by basic tools, the replanting of native species, the soil preparation, the intensive work; and then, allowing the forest to recover after the removal of invasive species, for it to settle again and for forest succession to take place over time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But given our physical constraints and scarce land area, there will be some greenfield sites that we might have to develop to meet our land use needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Any decision to proceed is made only after detailed study of the trade-offs and alternatives, including the assessment of ecological and biodiversity value.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And where development cannot be entirely avoided, we proceed with care.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Developments near to sites with significant biodiversity undergo an in-depth consultation with technical agencies and may be subject to an environmental study to assess the possible environmental impact of development plans, including ecological connectivity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We also engage stakeholders, such as those from the nature community, to take in feedback and strengthen the rigour of the studies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Unless there are security considerations, the studies will be made publicly available, so that anyone can provide feedback on the findings and recommendations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The studies, as well as feedback received, guide the planning of the site, including mitigating measures to reduce the impact on the environment where necessary.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We also seek to preserve and integrate natural elements within the development where possible, to facilitate ecological connectivity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We thank our nature groups and the nature community for their close partnership in working with the relevant agencies to achieve these outcomes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some called Ulu Pandan "Dover", but, of course, according to the planners, it is part of Ulu Pandan.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, let me use in Parliament the correct planning language.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The site at Clementi was an abandoned rubber plantation, which has since been overgrown with Albizia trees which are not native.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In January this year, I explained to Parliament that the land had been rezoned "Residential (Subject to Detailed Planning)" 23 years ago, since the Master Plan 1998.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This will give our future generations the option of deciding whether to use it for housing as intended by generations gone by, or to review its land use if the need arises.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As for the site at Ulu Pandan, it used to be a rubber plantation, fruit orchards and kampongs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In fact, I took a photographer of a marker and had a good discussion with heritage buffs, who are continuing to study what the history of that site was.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Because underlying all of Singapore, every inch of land, there are layers of history, layers of heritage, many stories to tell over the generations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The Ulu Pandan site is similarly overgrown with non-native trees after the rubber plantations, fruit orchards and kampongs were abandoned and the land taken by Government.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Since the Master Plan 2003, the land had been zoned "Residential (Subject to Detailed Planning)".

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: HDB then consulted nature groups to refine their plans for Ulu Pandan, incorporating the findings from the EBS.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Subsequently, the EBS report was published online to invite public feedback.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: HDB has since received and continues to receive feedback and suggestions from nearby residents, members of the public and those interested in nature and environmental issues.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There has been a very wide range of views and we thank everyone for contributing them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some have called to retain the site fully for greenery and recreation and to designate it as a Nature Park.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Others say keep it green but let us intervene through restoration.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, different levels of scientific understanding and interests.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Some have gone further to say that we should not build any more flats and halt all development.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Others have urged the Government to redevelop other sites instead, including vacant sites, acquiring older private or public housing or taking existing school fields, running tracks, car parks in the vicinity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Several have suggested that new housing and nature should co-exist on the site.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, develop parts that are less vegetated or with more non-native species.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: While there are diverse views and what I have just summarised is really just scratching the surface, many who have written in appreciate the tension between the need for development and nature conservation; and actually, all of them lie along a continuum of where that balance should lie.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are studying the feedback in detail and welcome more Singaporeans to give their views and inputs – give us your ideas, sketch them on a map – as we consider our plans for the Ulu Pandan site.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are encouraged by the keen interest generated in our plans for Singapore and nature conservation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Indeed, mainstreaming of nature consciousness or having conversations about conservation among Singaporeans at large is a key part of our strategy to become a City in Nature.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I talked about it in an interview with The Straits Times and, really, it is beyond just the locations and the science and conservation, but about mainstreaming these conversations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is a good time as concerns about sustainability are now at the top of our agenda.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: At the same time, as part of such conversations, it is good for all of us to better understand the opportunities and constraints facing Singapore when it comes to balancing our various land use needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And if we recalibrate the balance between conservation and development, or for that matter, between different kinds of developments and needs, or adjusting the ratio of different land use types, we should also need to discuss what this would mean, in practical terms.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For instance, I read in a TODAY commentary over the weekend, which quoted a 24-year old SUSS student Mr Yeo Wei Jiang who shared his personal convictions and some of those in his generation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: He said that preserving the natural environment should be Singapore's "top priority" and that, I quote, "I am willing to commit to it even if it means waiting longer for a BTO, living in a more inconvenient area, or paying a higher price".

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Singaporeans' aspirations and views are evolving: on housing, property, on material pursuits, on family and society, on nature and on the nature and form of work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: At the same time, the world and the global economy around us and technology are changing and changing rapidly – and so too must our strategies and approaches so that we can emerge as a stronger nation after this most difficult of tests.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We invite everyone to join these conversations and to partner us in action.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I want to thank Minister for the very comprehensive reply.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I think Minister touched on a very important concept which is the one about recycling and reuse of land.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I think that is critical as we balance the demands and needs of our population across generations.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I have two supplementary questions for the Minister.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The first is, we know that typically, there is a time lag between the planning and execution of projects, especially for the longer term projects.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: How does the Ministry make adjustments during this period, between planning and execution, as new factors arise due to the changing social structures, and also for the fact that there is global impact in the short term?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The second question is, if further assessments are made at any specific point of time, and we find that the ecological value and connectivity of the green sites have changed, what will the Ministry do with the original plans?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I think the Member makes a very important point that planning is not done on paper.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It involves visiting the site, doing lots of tests, looking at the surrounding community and their needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And then, from a decision point that we need to prepare for some need – whether industrial, housing, social community – to when it actually can start operating, it is quite a few years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And as more considerations, checks, tests, sampling and analysis need to be done in consultation, then, that time will grow longer and longer.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And remember that over that period of time, a lot of factors may change and there are many moving parts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: During that kind of timeframe, whether it is years or decades, things may change, including demographic structures, social need, demand may fluctuate depending on economic considerations and, of course, people's values and principles in what they feel is important here and now, and in the future.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And therefore, because we have had the privilege over the decades since our Independence for stability and continuity, our Public Service, together with the political leadership, have been able to put in place plans but also alternatives and contingencies – what if it is this; what if it is that.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And that is really our mindset – because we are not developers; we are stewards.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We provide the needs for Singaporeans, even those not yet born.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And if changes are made to certain plans, then, sometimes, we squeeze in one location, the problem pops up somewhere else.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Then, the question is – we talked about ecological prioritisation of biodiverse sites, or even the decision points on whether to redevelop or recover land from settlement or business, to recycle them, when and where we do so – there will be those implications.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But in essence, our demands are tied for today and tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We have to keep in mind the future generations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We must remember that things can change along the way.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And thanks to long-term planning by our planners and our leaders of days gone by, we seek to continue that mantle of responsibility.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We hope to be able to make those adjustments.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Just want to ask one clarification to the Minister, please.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The Minister shared about the assessments for green corridor connectivity.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can I just clarify with the Minister that when these assessments are made, especially when an environmental impact assessment is commissioned, the assessment looks not just at the plot of land under consideration, but also at the implications for the rest of the network of biodiversity if a particular node is developed?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I invite the Member to clarify, when he mentioned green corridor connectivity, are you talking about general ecological connectivity or the connectivity of the Green Corridor, the Rail Corridor?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I just want to be clear because the Rail Corridor runs through your constituency too, I believe.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: I am asking both specifically as well as more generally.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: Just want to clarify that we are looking at the broader impact to the network as well.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And it is for many, many users – it is for runners, joggers, cyclists, hikers, families, young people, seniors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is for communities of gardeners and farmers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And the different stretches of the Rail Corridor can also serve as ecological connectivity, for dispersal of flora, for fauna connectivity, whether it is insects, odonates, whether it is mammals, large or mostly small, to be able to then, also play that part in connecting different biodiversed core areas.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And, more broadly, it is the same concept as well.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And, in fact, in our conversations with our nature community – because our relationship has evolved and strengthened over time into a constructive and deep one – we are beginning to ask ourselves: should we just be looking at individual sites or should we be looking at the overall ecological map of Singapore?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: That map is very different from your urban map, I can assure you; very, very different.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And in our EIAs or EBSes, we do study the impact on connectivity between different areas.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We look at the impact on a whole range of issues that also impact the urban environment as much as we look at the environmental impact.
